title: Two Sum
followUps: What are the time and space complexities of your solution? Could you trade space for time or vice versa?
How would your approach change if the input array were already sorted?
How would you return every distinct pair of values that sums to the target instead of just one pair?
What if the array were too large to fit in memory on one machine?

interviewer.approach: Single pass with a hash map from value to index: for each x, check whether target - x was already seen. O(n) time, O(n) space. Brute force is O(n^2). The sorted variant can use two pointers in O(1) extra space.
hints: What is the brute-force approach, and what is its complexity? Where is the repeated work?
For each number, you know exactly which other value you need. How could you check whether you have already seen it in O(1)?
Try storing each value's index in a hash map as you scan, and checking for the complement before inserting.
pitfalls: Using the same element twice (e.g. target 6 with a single 3).
Inserting into the map before checking the complement, which breaks the duplicate-values case.
Sorting the array and losing the original indices.

dimensions.name: Scrutinising the AI's edge cases
dimensions.signals: Checked AI-written code against duplicate values ([3,3] with target 6), an element pairing with itself, negatives and zeros; noticed if the AI sorted the array and lost the original indices, or returned values or 1-based indices instead of 0-based indices.

levels.1: Adopted AI code that fails on duplicates or returns the wrong thing, without noticing.
levels.2: Ran the samples only; an AI edge-case bug survived or was found by accident.
levels.3: Tested the duplicate and self-pairing cases deliberately and fixed or confirmed the AI's handling.
levels.4: Predicted where the AI's code could break before running it and proved it with targeted inputs.

watchFor: Returning the two values, or 1-based indices, instead of the 0-based indices.
A sort + two-pointer answer that loses the original indices.
Inserting into the map before checking for the complement, so an element pairs with itself (target 6 with a single 3).
Claiming O(n) for a nested-loop solution, or O(1) space for the hash-map one.
